newsitem.title: USA: IMC expects 10-yr highs in corn, soy acres.
newsitem.headline: IMC expects 10-yr highs in corn, soy acres.

text.p: Fertilizer producer IMC Global Inc said its annual survey of U.S. planting intentions indicated farmers will plant 81 million acres of corn and 66 million acres of soybeans in 1997.
The corn plantings would be up two percent on last year and soybean plantings up four percent, with both projected planting levels the highest in at least 10 years, IMC said.
The U.S. Agriculture Department will issue its first estimate of 1997 corn and soybean plantings on March 31.

Last year, U.S. farmers planted 79.5 million acres to corn, harvesting 73.1 million and producing 9.293 billion bushels. Farmers planted 64.2 million acres to soybeans and harvested 63.4 million to produce 2.382 billion bushels.

IMC said its data was based on a survey of 1,000 farmers from nine states in the U.S. Corn Belt who together planted more than 1.5 million acres last year, at an average 800 acres of corn and 650 acres of soybeans.

"Our survey shows the largest corn acreage increases should be in the eastern Corn Belt, where we expect about a four percent improvement over 1996 with the states of Ohio and Indiana up 14 and 10 percent respectively," said IMC chairman Wendell F. Bueche.

IMC said the survey indicated that while 70 percent of Corn Belt farmers applied crop nutrients to fields last fall, about two-thirds of the respondents fertilized less acreage than a year earlier due to a late harvest and early winter.
So nitrogen, potash and phosphate application rates this spring should be equal or slightly above a year ago, IMC said.

"Overall, given historically low world grain stocks, the elimination of government-mandated planting restrictions, record farm income and favorable crop prices, the outlook remains very promising for strong crop nutrient demand not only in 1997, but also in 1998," Bueche said.
